U.A. Academy.text: Japan's national hero academy: a three-year residential program for high-school graduates, who all live in the Heights Alliance dorms on its walled campus above Musutafu. Principal Nezu, a white-furred animal with a genius intellect, runs it, and its teachers are working pro heroes: Shota Aizawa (Eraser Head), Present Mic, Nemuri Kayama, Cementoss, Ectoplasm, Thirteen, Power Loader, Recovery Girl and, from this April, All Might. It has four courses: Hero, General Studies, Support and Management. The Hero Course takes only two classes a year; at the televised Sports Festival, agencies scout students and General Studies students can earn a transfer. Outsiders see the country's best hero academy. The visible contradiction: the academy that trains the public's protectors locks the public out.

Hero Public Safety Commission.text: The government body that runs the hero system. It writes the rules for hero work, issues and revokes hero licenses, runs the Provisional Hero License Exam and coordinates heroes with the police. It also manages how the public sees heroes: it releases incident statistics, handles press relations and presents the twice-yearly Hero Billboard Chart JP, which ranks heroes by incidents resolved, public approval and social contribution. Its tower in central Tokyo is quiet, efficient and closed to visitors beyond the licensing counter. Heroes depend on it and rarely love it; to most citizens it is a seal on a license. The visible contradiction: a public-safety agency that worries about approval ratings as much as about safety.

Japanese Police.text: The prefectural police forces under the National Police Agency: patrol officers, detectives, traffic and riot units, custody officers and prisoner transport. They investigate crimes, secure scenes, take statements and make arrests, but officers do not use their Quirks as weapons, so they rely on licensed heroes to stop villains in a fight. A typical incident ends with a hero restraining someone and an officer snapping on the handcuffs. Detective Naomasa Tsukauchi is a familiar face around Musutafu. Most people trust the police and barely notice them. The visible contradiction: officers hold the legal power to arrest, question and detain, yet heroes get the headlines, the rankings and the credit.

League of Villains.text: A villain group so new and small that almost no one has heard of it. Its leader, Tomura Shigaraki, is a gaunt, restless young man who wears severed hands on his face and body, scratches his neck when frustrated and talks about villainy in video-game terms. Kurogiri, a polite man of dark mist whose Quirk opens warp gates, manages him, tends their hideout bar and moves people in and out. The rest are hired thugs found through brokers, and the man Shigaraki calls Sensei backs them all. Their aim is to kill All Might and bring down the hero society he holds up. The few brokers who deal with them see a strange client with money and big talk. The visible contradiction: a League with two real members at the start of the year, led by a man who has never led anyone.

Shie Hassaikai.text: One of the last yakuza houses in Japan, based in an old walled compound on the southeastern edge of Osaka. When heroes rose, they and the police broke the old crime families; the survivors were labeled designated villain groups and watched, and the Hassaikai has lasted by keeping its head down. Its old boss lies in a coma, and the house is run in his name by his young second, Kai Chisaki, called Overhaul: a cold, meticulous man in a beaked plague-doctor mask who cannot stand being touched and calls Quirks a sickness. His enforcers, the Eight Bullets, answer to him alone. Outsiders see a fading relic of the old underworld. The visible contradiction: everything is done in the boss's name, and the boss cannot speak.

Meta Liberation Army.text: A militant movement from the early years of the Quirk era. Led by a man called Destro, it demanded the right to use Quirks freely, calling every restriction an attack on a person's own body, and fought the government until it was crushed. Destro died in prison and the army was disbanded; today it shows up in documentaries and textbooks as a warning about Quirk extremism. Destro's writings still circulate among Quirk-rights activists and the curious. Officially it has had no members, no attacks and no leadership for decades, and most people file it under history. The visible contradiction: its central claim, that people should be free to use the power they were born with, still gets a sympathetic hearing on talk shows and online forums.

Wild Wild Pussycats.text: A team of four pro heroes specializing in mountain rescue: Mandalay, whose Quirk lets her speak into many people's minds at once; Pixie-Bob, who shapes earth into moving beasts; Ragdoll, who can locate up to a hundred people and read their condition; and Tiger, a hard-hitting martial artist who can bend his body freely. They wear matching cat-themed costumes, strike a team pose whenever they introduce themselves and have worked together for well over a decade. Their lodge sits on their own land, a huge stretch of the Japanese Alps northwest of Musutafu, which U.A. uses for summer training camps. Outsiders see a cheerful, slightly old-fashioned idol team. The visible contradiction: behind the cat ears and the pose, most of their work is grim searches for people lost in the mountains.

Endeavor Hero Agency.text: The agency of Endeavor (Enji Todoroki), the Number Two hero at the start of the year, run from a tower in central Tokyo. Endeavor holds the record for the most incidents resolved in Japan's history, and the agency is built for volume: dozens of sidekicks on rotating shifts, an operations floor that tracks incidents across the city in real time, and a training gym where everyone is expected to keep pace. Sidekicks such as Burnin, Kido and Onima work in his shadow and know that his standards do not bend. The public respects his results and does not much like him: he ignores fans, refuses interviews he considers pointless and treats second place as an insult. The visible contradiction: the country's most effective hero is also one of its least loved.

Shiketsu Academy.text: The great hero academy of western Japan and U.A.'s closest rival: people speak of U.A. in the east and Shiketsu in the west. It trains high-school graduates over three years and is nearly as hard to enter. Its students wear dark formal uniforms with peaked caps, keep strict manners in public and train in rescue, teamwork and public conduct as hard as in combat; Shiketsu teaches that a hero's image is part of the job. Its first-years include Inasa Yoarashi, a huge, loud young man with a powerful wind Quirk who turned down a place at U.A. Outsiders see polished, reliable future heroes. The visible contradiction: an academy built on composure and modesty puts real energy into proving it is better than U.A.

Villain Brokers.text: Not one organization but a trade: the middlemen of Japan's underworld. Brokers sell introductions between villains and clients, rent out safe rooms and hideouts, supply forged IDs, unregistered support gear and weapons, and find hired muscle for anyone who pays. They work by burner phone from bar back rooms and pawnshops in port and nightlife districts. The best known is Giran, a smooth, sharp-dressed broker who has outlasted most of his clients by never taking sides. The police know many brokers' names and can prove little. To the few outsiders aware of them, brokers are shady businessmen. The visible contradiction: brokers rarely commit a crime themselves, yet almost no villain operation happens without one.

Hawks Hero Agency.text: The agency of Hawks, the Number Three hero at the start of the year, based in Fukuoka. Hawks is the youngest hero ever to reach the top ten: a quick, easygoing man in his mid-twenties with large crimson wings whose feathers he can detach and steer one by one, fine enough to sense vibrations and strong enough to carry people. He is so fast that his own sidekicks often arrive only to file the paperwork. The agency is small and lean: a handful of sidekicks, a dispatch desk and a press office answering questions about cases he closed an hour ago. Fans love his relaxed manner and his line that he wants a world where heroes have free time. The visible contradiction: the hero who talks about slowing down is the fastest worker in the country.

The Age of Quirks.text: Generations ago, a baby was born in Qingqing City, China, glowing with a soft light. It was the first superhuman birth the world widely heard about, and within a few years similar reports came from everywhere. Children began manifesting powers that came to be called Quirks: flight, fire, extra limbs, strange senses. Laws, jobs, sports and insurance had all been built for ordinary bodies, and the old order cracked. Crime by people with powers grew faster than the police could answer it, governments struggled to keep control, and much of society's energy went into holding itself together. In that disorder some people used their powers to protect others with no legal right to do so. The state eventually answered with a system: Quirk registration, laws against public Quirk use and a licensed profession of heroes paid and regulated by the government. In Japan the Hero Public Safety Commission runs that system, and it has become the center of public life. Today about four in five people have a Quirk, and almost nobody alive remembers a world without them. Heroes are public servants, celebrities and the national ideal at once; children grow up with hero figures and ranking shows, and the hero academies are among the most competitive schools in the country. The chaotic early decades survive in textbooks and documentaries, and they remain the reason the rules exist: every restriction on Quirk use is the state's answer to the years when anyone with a dangerous power could do as they pleased.

Quirk Genetics and Inheritance.text: Quirks run in families. A child's Quirk usually takes after one parent's, mixes features of both, or turns out as something new that grows out of the family's traits. The child of a parent who hardens their skin and a parent who breathes underwater may inherit either power, a blend of the two or something neither parent has. Mutation happens too: parents with ordinary-looking bodies can have a heteromorph child, or a child with a power that has no clear family source, and doctors treat this as normal variation. Families with famous Quirks draw close attention from the press and from agencies watching for the next generation of talent. Choosing a partner for the power a child might inherit is called a Quirk marriage. It was common in the early generations and some old families still arrange them quietly, but the public now treats the practice as a scandal: marrying for a Quirk means treating a spouse and children as a breeding project, and any public figure suspected of it pays in reputation. Most families simply hope a child's Quirk turns out safe, useful and easy to live with. No test can promise a particular result before a child is born, and two siblings raised in the same house can have entirely different powers.

Quirk Singularity Theory.text: A fringe theory, discussed more often in pop-science books and late-night talk shows than in policy, holds that Quirks grow stronger, more complex and harder to control with each generation. Its supporters point to children whose powers outstrip both parents', to blended Quirks that combine several family traits, and to the number of young children who need specialist help to keep their Quirks in check. Their prediction is grim: at some point Quirks will outgrow the bodies that carry them, and a generation will be born that cannot control its own powers at all. Most scientists dismiss the theory as alarmism. They note that the data are thin, that strong Quirks are easier to notice than weak ones, and that better counseling and training have kept childhood accidents in check. The theory has no official standing: the government does not plan around it, hero academies do not teach it as fact, and its proponents carry little weight in their fields. It survives on online forums and in the occasional documentary, and people bring it up again whenever a child's Quirk causes a disaster on the evening news. For most people it is an unsettling idea that is easy to set aside.

Quirklessness.text: About one in five people have no Quirk, and the share is smaller among the young. Doctors can usually confirm it in early childhood with an X-ray of the foot: a little toe with a single joint is the common modern pattern and goes with a Quirk, while two joints is the older human pattern and almost always means no Quirk will ever appear. Families often take the diagnosis hard, because hero culture shapes childhood. A Quirkless child is pitied by adults and often teased or bullied by other children, and one who still wants to be a hero is usually told to give up the idea. No law bars Quirkless people from any job, school or exam, and most live ordinary lives as office workers, teachers, doctors, engineers, police officers and parents. Many grandparents are Quirkless and think nothing of it. The barriers are quieter: a teacher's lowered expectations, a sports club that assumes a power, a careless joke at a party, a job interview that drifts toward what the applicant cannot do. Hero work is the one field where the gap is real, since a professional hero has to face people with dangerous Quirks, and no Quirkless hero holds a high ranking. Quirkless adults who choose rescue, police or support work rely on training, gear and judgment, and they earn respect slowly.

Quirk Types.text: People sort Quirks into three broad types, and the words appear on school forms, in news reports and in everyday talk. Emitter Quirks produce or control something beyond the normal body: fire, electricity, ice, sound, force, a change in gravity, a substance released from the skin. Most Emitters switch on and off at will and work at a distance, and their limits show up as fuel, range or strain. Transformation Quirks change the body for a time: hardened skin, a larger size, a beast form, a body of liquid or metal. The user chooses when to change, and the change ends in fatigue, hunger or a vulnerable recovery period. Mutant Quirks are permanent features of the body: an animal head, gills, extra arms, a tail, wings, unusual eyes. They are always present, and any special function they carry comes from the body itself. The categories overlap at the edges and are rough tools, not a ranking. A weak-looking Quirk can be decisive in the right job, and a flashy one can be nearly useless indoors. Counselors, teachers and agencies care less about the category than about the specifics: what triggers a Quirk, what it costs, how long it lasts and how much of it the user's body can handle.

Heteromorphs and Prejudice.text: People whose Mutant Quirks give them visibly nonhuman bodies are called heteromorphs: animal heads, scales, stone skin, extra limbs, wings, tails. Cities have grown used to them. Some trains have wider doors and reinforced seats, clothing makers sell cuts for tails, wings and extra arms, and heteromorph pros can be national stars; Gang Orca, a top hero with the head and strength of an orca, is known across the country. Accommodation is still uneven: a uniform that does not fit, a helmet built only for a human head, a clinic without the right equipment, a public bath that turns away anyone with scales. Prejudice runs hardest in some isolated rural towns, where heteromorph children can be shunned, kept at home or blamed for bad luck, and adults who grew up that way often carry the scars long after they move away. In the cities the discrimination is quieter: an apartment that is suddenly taken when a heteromorph applicant arrives, a job interview that ends early, a stranger who changes seats on the train, an officer who questions the person with the frightening face first. Most heteromorphs want to be treated as individuals rather than as bodies. Many build ordinary lives, some turn their looks into an advantage in rescue or entertainment work, and a bitter few decide society will never accept them and stop trying. Activists push for better laws and design, and slurs that were common a generation ago now draw public criticism.

Quirk Registration and Counseling.text: Every Quirk in Japan is registered. When a child manifests a power, usually around age four, the family takes them to a doctor or a licensed Quirk counselor. The counselor examines the Quirk, gives it a working name and a description, notes its type, triggers and risks, and files it with the national registry. Children whose Quirk has not appeared by the usual age get a medical check, and the finding is recorded the same way. Counseling continues wherever a Quirk is dangerous to the child or to others: counselors teach control, safe habits and the law, and they advise parents and schools. Good counseling helps a child live with their power without shame; rigid counseling teaches a child to hide what they are, and some people resent it for life. Registry records follow a person into adulthood. A registered Quirk appears in school and hospital files, and employers may ask about it where safety depends on it. A Quirk that grows, changes or turns out to work differently than first thought should be updated, and updates for late developers are routine paperwork. The police and the Hero Public Safety Commission can consult the registry in an investigation, which is one reason Quirk criminals are often identified quickly. A private citizen cannot look up a stranger's Quirk, and the registry holds only what was reported to it.

Quirk Manifestation.text: Most Quirks appear in early childhood, usually by about age four. The first sign can be small: sparks from a fingertip, toys floating when a toddler cries, a sudden change in skin or hair. Mutant traits are often visible from birth and grow more pronounced over time. A first manifestation can be frightening and sometimes dangerous, and parents, preschools and pediatricians are trained to expect one. Late bloomers exist. A Quirk can stay hidden for years when its trigger never comes up, when it is too subtle to notice or when the body is not yet ready, and a rare few appear only in the teens or later. Doctors treat late onset as unusual but real, and the registry is updated when it happens. Quirks also grow. Strong emotion or sudden danger can push a Quirk past its usual limits for a moment, and everyone has heard stories of a power that doubled in a crisis. Those surges are real but costly and unreliable, and nobody builds a career on them. Steady growth comes from training, and it works at any age: control, range, output and endurance all improve with practice and a body conditioned to carry the power. Adults who begin serious training late can still make large gains, and hero academies expect every student's Quirk to change over three years of work.

Quirk Drawbacks and the Body.text: Every Quirk has a cost, because every Quirk runs through a body. Emitters strain whatever produces their effect: a fire user overheats, a sound user strains their throat, a user who burns body fat, sugar or water runs dry and has to eat or drink, an electric user who overloads is left dazed and slow. Transformations end in fatigue, soreness or a vulnerable recovery period. Mutant bodies can need more food, special care or gear built for them. Some Quirks have recoil: a power stronger than its user's frame can tear muscle or break bone with each use. Others come with conditions: a maximum duration, a cooldown, a trigger that needs line of sight, a sense lost while the Quirk is active. Pushing past a limit is possible and dangerous, and a hero who ignores the cost is called reckless, not brave. Bodies adapt. Repeated, careful use builds tolerance, and training the muscles, lungs and nerves around a Quirk raises its safe ceiling. Hero academies track each student's limits, and at U.A. Academy Recovery Girl heals injuries by drawing on the patient's own stamina, so even treatment costs something. Support gear manages many drawbacks with cooling layers, recoil-absorbing gauntlets and supply packs. No training or gear removes a drawback entirely, and the most respected pros are the ones who know exactly where their own limits lie.

Quirk Training and Technique.text: Professional heroes treat a Quirk as a skill. Training starts with control: switching the Quirk on and off cleanly, aiming it, holding it steady while moving and using it under stress without hurting allies. Then come output and endurance. Many heroes think of output as a dial rather than a switch and train to use exactly as much power as a situation needs; some measure it as a percentage of their maximum and drill holding fixed levels. Hero training also builds the body, since stronger muscles, lungs and bones raise what a Quirk can safely do. From that base heroes develop special moves: named, rehearsed techniques that apply a Quirk in one reliable way, such as a long-range shot, a burst of speed, a restraining hold or a wide-area rescue technique. The name helps a hero call up the move under pressure and lets teammates read it instantly. Special moves never add a power the Quirk lacks; they are practiced uses of what it already does. Support gear is the other half. Heroes work with designers to build costumes and equipment around their Quirks: nozzles that focus a spray, armor that carries recoil, tools that cover a weakness. Hero academies teach all of this as a curriculum, with specialist teachers, measured tests and regular drills, and pros keep training for their whole careers.

Quirk Suppression.text: A few Quirks can stop other Quirks. They are rare and highly valued, and their holders are recruited by hero academies, the police and the Hero Public Safety Commission; most end up as heroes or in custody work. Each suppression Quirk has its own conditions, such as eye contact, touch or range, and none of them works on everyone or for long. Suppression stops a power from being activated; it does not change a mutant body, which stays as it is. For everyone else, holding a Quirk criminal depends on equipment and procedure. Police carry restraints built for common Quirk types: heavy cuffs, full-hand mitts that block palm-based Quirks, blindfolds and muzzles for Quirks that work through sight or voice, sealed suits for gas and liquid users. A captured villain is restrained, identified against the registry and assessed for what their Quirk can do before transport. Prisoner vehicles and holding cells are built around the most common risks. Dangerous prisoners go to specialized facilities where cells, routines and guards are arranged around each inmate's Quirk, and the worst go to Tartarus. Sedation is used in emergencies under a doctor's order. Every form of suppression is temporary, and every holding system depends on staff who know exactly what each prisoner can do.

Hero Licensing System.text: Only licensed heroes may use their Quirks in public as a profession: to fight villains, carry out rescues and act in emergencies. The Hero Public Safety Commission issues every license. A full hero license usually follows graduation from an accredited hero course and the Commission's requirements; a provisional license, earned through a separate exam, gives students limited emergency authority while they train. Every licensed hero registers a hero name with the Commission. The name is public and becomes the hero's working identity: costume, agency, merchandise and news coverage all use it, and many heroes keep their legal names out of the press. Hero Course students choose their hero names in class during their first year, and some change them later. A license is a legal status, not a rank. It allows a hero to use their Quirk on duty, to restrain and detain suspects until the police arrive and to direct civilians in an emergency. It does not allow punishment of suspects, unnecessary force or investigations beyond the hero's role, and heroes answer for misconduct the same way other public officials do. The Commission can suspend or revoke a license for criminal acts, reckless damage, serious misconduct or failure to meet its standards, and a hero who loses a license loses the legal right to work. Licensed heroes also carry duties: reporting incidents, cooperating with the police and keeping their registered information current.

Hero Law and Quirk Use.text: In Japan, using a Quirk in public is legal only in narrow cases. Licensed heroes may use their Quirks on duty. Everyone else may use a Quirk in private, at work where the job and its permits allow it, and in supervised training at a school or licensed facility. Small, harmless everyday uses in public are tolerated in practice, but anything that could injure someone or damage property counts as misuse. Using a Quirk against another person is the line the law cares about most. A civilian who attacks with a Quirk is a criminal, and the press and the police call that person a villain whatever the motive. Self-defense is the main exception: a person may use a Quirk to escape an immediate attack, with only the force needed. Stepping in to save someone else is a gray zone. Police and courts weigh how urgent the danger was, whether a hero or officer was present and how much force and damage followed; the usual result is a statement and a warning, sometimes a fine, and a charge when someone gets hurt. Fighting a villain without a license, chasing a suspect or patrolling as a vigilante is illegal even when it ends well. Penalties run from warnings and fines to arrest, prison and a criminal record that can bar a person from ever holding a hero license. Hero students are bound by the same laws: on campus and under a teacher's supervision they may train freely, but off campus they have no more authority than any other citizen until they earn a provisional license.

Hero Billboard Chart JP.text: The Hero Billboard Chart JP is the official ranking of Japan's professional heroes, published by the Hero Public Safety Commission twice a year. It weighs three things: incidents resolved, social contribution and public approval. Combat strength is not a category, so a quiet rescue specialist can outrank a famous brawler, and a popular hero with few cases can slide. The full chart runs far down the list of active heroes, but public attention goes to the top ten, announced at a televised event with speeches, interviews and heavy press coverage. A ranking moves an agency's fortunes: a rise brings sponsors, sidekick applicants, fan mail and bigger cases, and a fall can cost all of them. At the start of this academic year the order at the top is long familiar. All Might is Number One and has held the top spot for so long that most young people cannot remember anyone else there; his lead over the field is enormous. Endeavor is Number Two, with the most incidents resolved in history and approval numbers far below his results. Hawks is Number Three, the youngest hero ever to reach the top ten. Fans argue about the rest constantly, on talk shows, in school hallways and on online forums, and predicting the next chart is a national pastime. Pros publicly claim not to care about their numbers, and most of them check anyway.

Hero Agencies and Sidekicks.text: Most professional heroes work through hero agencies. An agency is a licensed business led by a pro hero: it keeps an office, hires sidekicks and staff, covers a patrol area, answers emergency calls and handles press and merchandise. Agencies range from one-hero offices on a shopping street to towers with dozens of sidekicks, dispatch floors and private gyms. Sidekicks are licensed heroes employed by another hero's agency. Many are young pros gaining experience before opening their own offices; others stay for a whole career because they prefer teamwork to running a business. The lead hero answers for the agency's sidekicks in the field, and a famous lead hero's reputation carries the whole office. Pay comes from several sources. The government pays heroes for public service according to the cases they resolve and the help they give, so case credit matters: when several heroes work one incident, who made the capture or the rescue goes on record, and disputes over credit are common. Agencies also earn from merchandise, endorsements and appearance fees. Heroes team up for large incidents, either through operations planned with the police or by calling in allies from nearby agencies, and the hero leading the operation assigns the roles. Students meet agencies through internships and work-studies. Graduating Hero Course students apply to agencies the way other graduates apply for jobs, and the ambitious open their own offices once their reputations allow it.

Internships and Work-Studies.text: Hero academies use two kinds of field placement. Internships come first. After the U.A. Sports Festival, agencies that watched the broadcast send offers to the Hero Course students they want, and each student picks one; students without offers choose from a standing list of agencies that take interns every year. Before going, students choose the hero names they will use in the field. An internship lasts about a week. Interns follow patrols, office work and training, wear their costumes in public under their mentor's supervision and help in emergencies only at the mentor's direction. Without a license they have no right to fight villains on their own, and the mentor answers for their safety. Work-studies come later and require a provisional license. A work-study student joins an agency for a term or longer and works real cases between classes, with the academy's permission and under the agency's supervision. Work-study students carry more responsibility than interns, and the academy can pull a student from a placement if it judges the work unsafe or the student's studies suffer. Not every agency accepts students, and many prefer trainees who have already shown what they can do. For agencies, students are a scouting pipeline: a good intern or work-study student often returns after graduation as a sidekick.

Underground Heroes and Vigilantes.text: Underground heroes are licensed professionals who avoid publicity on purpose. They turn down interviews, skip merchandise deals, work mostly at night or undercover and rarely appear near the top of the Hero Billboard Chart JP. Their work is surveillance, tracking, infiltration and the capture of villains who would see a famous face coming. Obscurity is part of the method: a villain who does not know a hero's Quirk cannot plan against it. The public barely knows their names, while the police and other pros know them well. Fans tend to think of them as eccentrics; inside the profession they are respected. Vigilantes are a different matter. A vigilante is anyone who acts as a hero without a license: patrolling, stopping crimes or fighting villains on their own authority. Under hero law that is a crime, even when the vigilante means well and even when the rescue succeeds, and the police treat vigilantes as offenders to be identified and arrested. The public is split. Some admire vigilantes as brave people filling gaps the heroes leave, especially in neighborhoods with few agencies, and every few years a local vigilante becomes an online celebrity. Others see dangerous amateurs whose fights wreck streets and get people hurt. Heroes generally side with the law, since the licensing system exists to keep untrained people from fighting in public, and good intentions do not reduce the risk.

Support Industry.text: Behind every pro hero stands the support industry. Support companies design and manufacture hero costumes, protective gear, tools and devices, each built around a specific Quirk and body: heat-resistant fabrics for fire users, gauntlets that store or channel a Quirk's output, goggles, capture weapons, breathing gear, grappling lines and armor. A large company may outfit dozens of agencies, while small workshops live on custom pieces. Hero gear is regulated. Equipment used in the field must meet government standards and be registered, and selling unregistered support gear, especially weapons, is a crime, though brokers trade it anyway. Hero Course students at U.A. Academy submit costume designs with their applications; the academy passes them to contracted support companies, which deliver working costumes for the start of hero training, and students revise them as their Quirks and techniques develop. Designers learn the trade in support courses at hero academies and engineering schools. At U.A. the Support Course trains them in the Development Studio under Power Loader, where students build, test and occasionally blow up prototypes, and the best pitch their work to companies at public events. Good support design starts from what a hero actually needs and respects what a body can take. Gear that covers a weakness is prized; gear that hides a weakness the wearer has not learned to manage is dangerous.

Hero Media and Fandom.text: Heroes are the biggest celebrities in Japan. News channels cover rescues live, with helicopters and street cameras racing to every major incident. Ranking shows, talk shows and variety programs fill the schedule with hero interviews, analysis and gossip, and each Hero Billboard Chart JP announcement is a national event. Merchandise is big business: figures, trading cards, posters, costume replicas, snacks and stationery carry heroes' faces and emblems, and All Might goods outsell everything else. Some heroes treat publicity as part of the job. Mount Lady built her name on headline-grabbing captures, Uwabami is as familiar from commercials as from patrols, and Best Jeanist is a fashion icon as well as a top hero. Others avoid cameras entirely, and Endeavor's refusal to play along is a story in itself. Fan culture is everywhere: fan clubs, collector shops, analysis blogs and forums, autograph lines, cosplay, children's lunch boxes. Many young people know heroes' Quirks, special moves and ranking histories by heart, and some keep detailed notebooks. The press shapes careers. A dramatic rescue on camera can make a rookie famous overnight, and a scandal, a careless comment or property damage on video can sink an approval rating within a week. Agencies keep press officers for that reason, and the Hero Public Safety Commission watches public opinion closely.

Police and Heroes.text: Japan's police and its heroes divide the work of public safety. Heroes respond to Quirk crimes, disasters and rescues, and they restrain villains with their Quirks. Police officers do not use their Quirks as weapons on duty; they secure scenes, investigate crimes, take statements, collect evidence, make formal arrests and hold suspects in custody. A hero's capture becomes a case only when the police take over: an officer makes the arrest, the hero gives a statement and the evidence enters the police chain of custody, never the hero's keeping. Heroes may not hold or interrogate suspects on their own. Cooperation works best at the local level, where patrol heroes and police stations know each other by name. For larger operations the police and agencies plan together: detectives build the case, then request heroes for the arrest, with a lead hero and a police commander sharing command. Detective Naomasa Tsukauchi, a familiar face around Musutafu, is one of the officers heroes most often work with. Friction exists. Heroes collect the headlines and the case credit while detectives do the slow work; police complain about heroes who wreck evidence, chase suspects across jurisdictions or treat officers as a cleanup crew; heroes complain about paperwork and slow warrants. The Hero Public Safety Commission coordinates heroes and police at the national level, and in daily practice most officers and pros respect each other's limits.

Rescue Priority and Collateral Damage.text: Hero work has a clear order: save lives first, then contain the danger, then capture the villain. A hero who chases a suspect past trapped civilians is failing at the job even if the capture succeeds, and the academies, the Commission and the public all judge heroes by that rule. The social contribution score on the Hero Billboard Chart JP rewards evacuations and rescues as well as captures, and rescue specialists are respected for it. Fights between Quirk users break things. Buildings crack, cars burn, roads split and water mains burst, and the bill is real. Agencies carry liability insurance, the government covers some damage done in the course of lawful hero work, and a hero whose force was reckless or unnecessary can face claims, Commission discipline and a drop in approval. Mount Lady is known for the damage her size leaves behind, and heroes with large-scale Quirks train hard in precision for the same reason. Public anger follows visible damage quickly. Shop owners and residents complain to the press, news programs replay the wreckage, and online commentators argue over whether a hero went too far. The same footage can make a hero famous if it shows people carried out alive. Hero academies drill these choices in disaster exercises, rescue tests and mock-city battles, grading students on whom they saved and what they broke as well as on what they defeated.

Hero Retirement.text: Pro heroes retire for the same reasons athletes do, and often for harder ones. Many leave when age slows them, since the job demands speed and stamina, and a body that once handled a Quirk easily can start to struggle with it. Injury ends many careers early: a single wound that makes fighting or a Quirk unsafe can force a hero out after one incident, and the public usually learns of it from a short press release. Others step away after a loss, a scandal or simple exhaustion. Retirement is a legal step: the hero notifies the Hero Public Safety Commission, which retires the license. An agency does not outlive its founder automatically. A senior sidekick may take over and run it under a new name, the staff may merge into another agency, or the office may close; fans, sponsors and the patrol area all have to be earned again by whoever stays. Retired heroes rarely disappear. Many teach at hero academies, train young pros privately, consult for agencies or the police, or appear as commentators on hero programs. The press covers the departure of any famous hero at length, and fans argue for months about who will fill the gap on the chart.

U.A. Admissions.text: U.A. Academy fills its Hero Course through two routes, both open only to high-school graduates. The general entrance exam runs each February. Applicants sit a written exam, then a practical one: a short, timed battle in one of the academy's mock cities against robot villains worth one, two or three points each, with Quirks allowed and teachers watching. A giant robot worth zero points roams each site as an obstacle, and the sensible move is to get away from it. The briefing mentions only villain points. A panel of teachers also awards rescue points from the control room for helping other applicants, and the two scores together decide the ranking. Recovery Girl treats the injured on site, and results arrive by mail about a week later. The odds are steep, often quoted at about three hundred applicants for each Hero Course place, and the robot practical favors Quirks that can break machines, a standing complaint among applicants whose powers work only on people. Many who miss the cut enter General Studies instead and keep their eyes on a transfer. The recommendation route is far smaller: applicants backed by their schools or by pro heroes take a separate practical test and an interview, and only a handful get in each year, usually two to each Hero Course class. A recommendation buys a test, not a place, and recommended students carry the expectation of being the best in their class. The General Studies, Support and Management courses admit through their own exams, weighted toward their own work. Principal Nezu approves every admission.

U.A. Courses.text: U.A. Academy runs four courses, and every first-year belongs to a lettered homeroom class. The Hero Course has two classes a year, 1-A under Shota Aizawa and 1-B under Vlad King, twenty students each and full from the first day (a player character enrolled in one sits beside the twenty as an extra student, so that class has twenty-one; nobody else is added): mornings of standard subjects, afternoons of Foundational Hero Studies in costume on the training grounds, and steady preparation for the Provisional Hero License Exam. General Studies (Classes 1-C to 1-E) gives a broad academic education with no hero training; many of its students sat the Hero Course exam and missed. The Support Course (1-F to 1-H) designs and builds gear in Power Loader's Development Studio and handles costume repairs and change requests for the Hero Course. The Management Course (1-I to 1-K) studies agency finance, contracts, publicity and media relations, and sees hero students as future clients. The courses share the same uniform, the same cafeteria and many of the same lecturers, but not the same standing: the Hero Course gets the cameras, and the rest of the academy notices. Movement between courses is real. A strong showing at the Sports Festival can earn a General Studies student a transfer into the Hero Course, and a Hero Course student who falls short can be moved out; teachers also hold the power to expel. The rivalry between 1-A and 1-B runs through every shared exercise. Each class has a class representative, and the third-year Hero Course includes the Big Three, the students the academy counts as its strongest.

Heights Alliance Dorms.text: Every U.A. Academy student lives on campus in Heights Alliance from the first day of the first year; nobody commutes. Each Hero Course class in all three years has its own five-story building, and the General Studies, Support and Management students share larger halls at the far end of the yard, with all three courses mixed on every floor. A Hero Course building has a ground-floor lounge with a big television, a kitchen and a dining table that seats the whole class, a laundry room and baths; upstairs, the men's and women's wings hold private rooms with a bed, desk, closet and balcony, which residents furnish as they please. The shared halls add quiet study rooms and a ventilated workroom for Support residents. The rules are simple and enforced. Curfew falls each night, faculty walk rounds after dark, and anyone caught outside after it earns house arrest and cleaning duty. Door readers log every entry. Leaving campus means signing out on the building's sheet, and the Main Gate passes students only when they are signed out; a missing sign-out reaches the homeroom teacher by morning. Residents may visit each other's rooms until curfew. Many go home on weekends, and the Sunday-evening return is the busiest hour at the gate. Cooking, cleaning and laundry run on rotas that every building argues over. The dorms make U.A. a whole life: classmates are neighbors, rivals share a kitchen, and nothing that happens in a lounge stays private for long.

U.A. Grounds and Facilities.text: U.A. Academy's grounds cover the forested hills directly above Musutafu, on Mount Fuji's eastern foothills; the Main Gate is about 3 kilometers northeast of Musutafu Station, ten minutes by city bus, and all of it is closed ground. The only way in from the city is the Main Gate in the security wall, where sensors read every student and faculty ID; anyone without one triggers the U.A. Barrier, thick steel panels that slam across the opening. Visitors need an appointment and an escort, and reporters wait outside the gate whenever U.A. is in the news. Inside, the H-shaped glass main building holds the homerooms, the Faculty Office, Recovery Girl's Infirmary, Power Loader's Development Studio and Lunch Rush's Cafeteria, with the Library and the Courtyard in front and Heights Alliance a short walk away. Behind the main campus the training grounds are spread through the forested hills, each behind its own wall and linked by winding campus roads and buses: Ground Beta and the six other mock cities (Battle Centers A to G, with Ground Beta as B), full-size streets and office blocks built for battle and rescue exercises; Training Ground Gamma, a cramped maze of pipes, tanks and catwalks; Gym Gamma, a concrete gym on the main campus that Cementoss reshapes into cliffs and pits; the Unforeseen Simulation Joint (USJ), Thirteen's rescue dome of flood, fire, landslide, storm, ruin and mountain zones, high in the forest at the top of the grounds; and U.A. Stadium, the great bowl beside the main campus that hosts the Sports Festival. Grounds are booked through the Faculty Office in afternoon blocks, and outside bookings they stand closed and empty. Damage is part of every lesson, and repair crews and Cementoss put the grounds back together afterward.

U.A. Faculty Life.text: Every U.A. Academy teacher is a licensed pro hero, and most still keep a hand in field work: Shota Aizawa (Eraser Head) patrols at night as an underground hero, Thirteen takes rescue operations, and All Might joined the faculty this April as the Number One hero at the start of the year. Principal Nezu, an animal whose Quirk gives him an intellect beyond any human's, runs the academy on a principle of freedom: teachers set their own methods, exercises and standards, and that freedom includes the power to expel a student judged to have no potential. Aizawa is known inside the academy for using it. Nezu decides admissions, transfers, expulsions and faculty hiring in the Principal's Office, usually over tea, and deals with the government and the Commission himself. Homeroom teachers take attendance at 8:30, run their class's hero training and answer for their students' conduct and safety, in class and in the dorms. Present Mic, Nemuri Kayama, Cementoss and Ectoplasm teach the morning subjects; Snipe, Power Loader, Vlad King and Hound Dog, the guidance counselor and disciplinarian, round out the staff, and Recovery Girl treats everyone. The duty of care is absolute: every exercise is supervised, a teacher stops any bout that turns dangerous, the injured go straight to Recovery Girl, and a real villain threat means evacuation, the Barrier and calls for backup, never a lesson. Faculty meet in the Faculty Office before homeroom, grade late and walk rounds at Heights Alliance after dark.

U.A. Sports Festival.text: The U.A. Sports Festival is the biggest sporting event in Japan. Once Quirks made fair international competition impossible, the Olympics shrank to a shadow of their old scale, and U.A.'s yearly festival took their place in public interest: every spring, crowds of tens of thousands and a national television audience watch the academy's students compete. Each year group has its own events, all four courses compete together within a year, and the first-year events in U.A. Stadium draw the biggest crowds because the faces are new. The preliminary events change every year and stay secret until the day, chosen by the chief referee; past festivals have opened with races, team battles and obstacle courses before narrowing the field to one-on-one bouts on a concrete stage that Cementoss raises in the arena. Nemuri Kayama has refereed the first-year events in recent years, and Present Mic calls them from the broadcast booth. Pro heroes fill reserved sections to scout, and the offers agencies send afterward decide where first-years spend their first workplace experience. For General Studies, Support and Management students it is the one stage the whole country watches: a strong General Studies showing can earn a Hero Course transfer, Support students show off their gear to the support companies, and Management students track who draws the cameras. Every bout is supervised and nonlethal; the referee stops a fight that turns dangerous, and Recovery Girl works from a treatment room under the stands. Students of other academies never compete, but many watch the broadcast.

U.A. Weekly Timetable.text: A U.A. Academy weekday runs on the chime. Heights Alliance residents cook or grab breakfast in their dorm kitchens and cross the Courtyard to homeroom at 8:30. Mornings belong to standard subjects for every course, four 40-minute periods in the homeroom (English at 9:15, modern literature at 10:00, math at 10:45, modern hero art history at 11:30): English with Present Mic, modern literature with Cementoss, math with Ectoplasm, modern hero art history with Nemuri Kayama, plus each course's own lectures. At the 12:30 bell the whole academy arrives at Lunch Rush's Cafeteria at once; Lunch Rush, the Cook Hero, serves first-rate set meals for about 500 to 800 yen, and the line reaches the doors within minutes. In the afternoon the courses split. Hero Course classes change into costume and board campus buses for Foundational Hero Studies at 13:30 on the training grounds, each class on its own rotation, until about 15:00; General Studies keeps lecturing until around four; Support students build in the Development Studio; Management students work through case studies. After classes come the Library, open until nine on weekdays, booked training, clubs, gear fittings and dinner shifts in the dorms, then curfew at 22:00. Weekends are free, with shorter Library hours, signed-out trips to town and visits home. Recovery Girl's Infirmary keeps class hours and is busiest when training ends. Her rules are fixed: her healing kiss speeds the body's recovery by spending the patient's own stamina, so a drained patient sleeps for hours; she rations it, scolds repeat visitors, sends serious cases to hospital and refuses further treatment, whoever objects, when a patient cannot take more. Exams, events and emergencies override the timetable while they run.

Rival Hero Academies.text: U.A. Academy is the most famous hero academy in Japan, not the only one. People speak of U.A. in the east and Shiketsu Academy in the west. Shiketsu is nearly as hard to enter, drills formal courtesy into students who wear dark uniforms with peaked caps, and trains rescue, teamwork and public conduct as hard as combat, on the principle that a hero's image is part of the job. Ketsubutsu Academy, whose hero course counts Ms. Joke, the Smile Hero, among its teachers, has a reputation for friendly manners off the field and shrewd, calculated play once a contest starts. Seiai Academy and smaller academies across the country complete the field. All of them follow U.A.'s pattern: three-year programs for high-school graduates, each with its own campus, uniform, rules and traditions. Their students meet U.A.'s at the Provisional Hero License Exam, the Commission's licensing test, and at occasional joint events. They never enter U.A.'s Sports Festival, which belongs to U.A. alone, but many watch its broadcast to scout future rivals and build strategies around the Quirks they see on television. The academies compete every winter for the best applicants, and a strong applicant may sit more than one entrance exam. Between academies the rivalry is mostly pride: Shiketsu students measure themselves against U.A. at every chance, and U.A. students learn quickly that a polite stranger from another academy may already know their Quirk. Until they hold a license, students of every academy are bound by the same Quirk law as everyone else.

The Hero Killer.text: Stain, called the Hero Killer by the press and the police, is the most wanted villain in Japan. Working alone, he has killed or crippled dozens of pro heroes across several cities, and as of the start of the year he has never been caught. His pattern is known from survivors and case files: he watches a city's heroes from its rooftops, chooses one, strikes at night in a narrow place, and is gone before backup arrives. He fights with knives and a sword. Survivors report that after the first cut they could not move, and police files hold no confirmed account of his Quirk. Survivors also say he calls his victims fakes, and investigators read his creed in his choices: a hero who works for money, fame or a ranking is a fraud, a true hero acts only to save others, and the fakes must be purged until the word hero means something again. Sightings describe a lean man with a scarred face, a long tattered red scarf and a cloth bandana, too few to give the public a clear picture. Detectives in several prefectures share his files, and the Hero Public Safety Commission reviews them with the police. Every new attack dents public trust in heroes and puts agencies on edge: pros double up on night patrols where they can, and talk shows argue over whether the system that ranks heroes by popularity created him. To most of the public he is a name on the news and a reason to be glad of a hero nearby.

Yakuza Remnants.text: Japan's yakuza did not survive the age of heroes intact. In the chaos when Quirks spread, the old crime families grew rich, but as licensed heroes rose and worked with the police, the families were broken one after another: bosses jailed, money seized, territories absorbed into agency patrol routes. The survivors were declared designated villain groups. Their membership is registered with the police, their offices and compounds are watched, and any crime by one member brings scrutiny on the whole group. Most members drifted into ordinary jobs or ordinary crime; a few houses held together around an old boss, a name and a code of loyalty. The remnants live small: gambling dens, loans at hard interest, protection money from shops that remember them, smuggling and the odd job through a broker, all kept quiet enough to stay below a hero's notice. They keep their ceremony: oaths sworn over sake cups, formal ranks, deference to the boss and a habit of settling disputes inside the house. The public sees them as relics, old men in old suits from a vanished era, and most heroes treat them as a police matter. The best known surviving house is the Shie Hassaikai, which keeps a walled compound on the southeastern edge of Osaka. A designated group that draws heroes to its door rarely survives the attention, so every house weighs its ambitions against that risk.

Trigger.text: Trigger is an illegal drug that boosts a Quirk. A single dose drives the user's Quirk far past its normal output within moments: an emitter's blast doubles in force, a strength Quirk tears through steel, a mutant body swells, hardens or grows past its usual shape. The cost comes with it. Users lose judgment and self-control, turn violent at small provocations and cannot measure their own power, so a petty thief on Trigger becomes a public emergency. The effect lasts a short time and leaves the user exhausted, often hurt by their own output, and sometimes with lasting damage to the body. Repeated use does not train a Quirk; it wears down the person using it. Possession and sale are crimes, and Quirk use under Trigger counts as villainy whatever the user meant. It moves through the underworld in small glass ampoules, sold in nightlife districts, back alleys and the port quarters of big cities by small-time dealers who rarely know who makes it. Police seizures have been rising in Kansai and around Tokyo, and pros who meet a sudden, oversized Quirk rampage now suspect Trigger first. Hospitals treat the aftermath; detectives try to work back up the chain from street sellers and seldom get far. For the desperate, the weak and the angry, it offers a few minutes of being strong, and that promise is what keeps it selling.

Tartarus.text: Tartarus is Japan's maximum-security prison for villains too dangerous for any ordinary facility. It is built into a small volcanic island among the Izu Islands, about 55 kilometers south of the Tartarus Transfer Port at the tip of the Izu Peninsula, behind high sea walls inside a police exclusion zone. It is a national facility: a guard force under the National Police Agency runs custody and transfers, and the Hero Public Safety Commission vets every member of staff and approves every visit. Its rules are absolute. Nobody lands without written authorization, and only by armored transfer boat or helicopter from the port. Each inmate lives alone in a cell deep inside the island, built around that inmate's Quirk, with restraints that block it and automatic guns covering the bed. Inmates leave a cell only in full restraints with an escort of four guards, and no door in the prison opens without two officers confirming it. Visits are approved weeks ahead, limited in time, recorded and held across a thick transparent wall, with the prisoner strapped into a fixed chair under guns that fire at any sign of Quirk use; a guard reads the rules aloud first, and the visit ends at the first breach. Guards work long rotations on the island in armored gear. Only the worst offenders are sent there: serial killers, villains whose Quirks no ordinary cell can hold, and criminals judged too dangerous to live among other prisoners. To the public, Tartarus is the end of the line.

Hosu.text: Hosu is a dense commuter city about 30 kilometers north of central Tokyo, half an hour out by express train, and it runs on the commuter clock. Elevated rail lines cross it in every direction on concrete overpasses. Platforms are packed at dawn and dusk, downtown goes quiet at midday, and izakaya and karaoke bars keep the side streets busy until the last train; after that the back lanes go dark and empty. Hosu Downtown is a grid of office towers, banks, a department store and chain restaurants along Main Street, which runs north from Hosu Station, with a police box and a giant news screen on the Station Plaza. Southwest of the station, the older quarter of the Hosu Back Alleys packs four- to six-story blocks wall to wall, with lanes too narrow for cars and rooftops crowded with water tanks and air-conditioning units, where residents dry laundry by day. Most people here are office workers, shopkeepers and families in aging apartment blocks. Hosu has few heroes for its size. The big agencies sit in central Tokyo, and a call from downtown can wait ten minutes or more for a pro, which shop owners complain about openly. Small local agencies share the patrols with the city police under Chief Kenji Tsuragamae: Manual runs a careful, by-the-book agency near the station, and Native walks Main Street on foot. Hosu General Hospital handles the city's emergencies, and patrol heroes with movement Quirks treat the rooftops as their fastest routes across town.

Japan's Regions.text: The world map is one true-scale map of central and western Japan, from northern Kyushu east along the Seto Inland Sea and the Kansai cities, across the Japanese Alps and the Tokai coast to Tokyo, the Boso Peninsula and the mountains of Niigata and Fukushima. Every square on it is about 60 kilometers across, so the gaps between places on the map are the real distances, and every square that is not part of the story is real Japanese country, town or sea, there to travel through. Musutafu, a Shizuoka city on Suruga Bay at the root of the Izu Peninsula, lies below U.A. Campus, the forested hill country on Mount Fuji's eastern foothills that holds U.A. Academy's walled grounds; its station is a shinkansen stop 45 minutes from Tokyo. South of it run Tartarus Coast, the Izu Peninsula's tip with the Tartarus Transfer Port, and Tartarus Waters, the open Pacific among the Izu Islands where the prison Tartarus stands alone on its island. Greater Tokyo, about 100 kilometers northeast of Musutafu, is the capital and the heart of the hero business: Tokyo Station, the Hero Public Safety Commission Headquarters, the agencies of Endeavor and Best Jeanist, avenues of hero billboards, and, about 30 kilometers north of the center, Hosu, a dense commuter city with elevated railways, crowded back alleys and too few heroes. Kamino and Yokohama, the bay shore southwest of the capital, pairs Yokohama's working port and Chinatown with Kamino Ward, a tired old ward of shuttered shops and idle warehouses, and Takoba Municipal Stadium, a venue for the Commission's license exam. Northwest of Tokyo, about 100 kilometers out in the mountains, lie Deika, a prosperous company town built around the support maker Detnerat below Gunga Mountain, and Jaku, a quieter basin city with the district's largest hospital. The Mountain Training Lands in the Kiso valley of the Japanese Alps, three to four hours by bus from Musutafu, are the private forest of the Wild Wild Pussycats, where U.A. holds its summer training camps. Osaka North and Osaka South, two hours west of Musutafu by shinkansen to Shin-Osaka Station, are Osaka and its neighbors Kyoto and Nara: canals, neon, covered arcades, the agencies of Fat Gum and Sir Nighteye, and one old yakuza compound. Kyushu, at the western end of the map, is Fukuoka and Hakata on the island's north coast, home of the Hawks Hero Agency, about 4.5 hours from Musutafu by shinkansen. Between them the map holds the real country: the Hokuriku coast and the Noto Peninsula on the Sea of Japan, the Japanese Alps and the volcanoes of Nagano and Gunma, Nagoya and the Tokai cities along the Pacific, the castle towns and ports of the Seto Inland Sea, Shikoku's mountains and capes, the San'in coast and the Oki Islands, and the seas around them. Getting between the story's cities still means a train, a bus, a ferry or a plane, and the trip takes the real time.

Provisional License Exam.text: The Provisional Hero License Exam is held by the Hero Public Safety Commission on a regular schedule at venues around the country, Takoba Municipal Stadium among them. Hero academies decide which students are ready to sit it; most wait until their students have more training behind them, though an academy can enter a first-year class early if it judges the class ready. Candidates from many schools, U.A. Academy and Shiketsu Academy included, compete at once, and far more sit the exam than pass. The format changes from year to year, but its shape is familiar: a large, competitive first stage that cuts the field down fast, then a practical stage, usually a staged disaster, where candidates are graded on rescue, triage, communication and judgment. Commission staff and trained actors play injured civilians and score the candidates directly, and a staged villain attack may break into the exercise. Strength alone does not pass. Candidates lose points for ignoring victims, taking needless risks or refusing to work with others. A provisional license lets a student use their Quirk in emergencies and take part in supervised hero work, including work-studies with agencies, but it is not a full license, and the holder still works under a supervising pro's responsibility. Candidates who fail the final stage may be offered the remedial course: special lectures and practical sessions run by the Commission over a few months, ending in a final assessment. Those who pass it receive the same provisional license.

The Symbol of Peace.text: All Might, the Symbol of Peace, has been Japan's Number One hero for decades and is the most famous person in the country. He arrives at disasters laughing, with the words "I am here," and the public credits him with a long fall in villain crime: many would-be villains stay quiet simply because he exists. His face is on billboards, cereal boxes, trading cards and children's pajamas, and Endeavor, the Number Two, has spent his whole career trying and failing to close the gap. At the start of the year All Might joined the faculty of U.A. Academy, his own alma mater, to teach Foundational Hero Studies; the news set off a media frenzy, and every hero fan in Japan wants to know what he teaches. In public he is huge, booming and theatrical, poses for every camera and answers every question with a joke; colleagues and students find him warm, encouraging and hopeless at paperwork. Villains speak of him with fear or hatred, and late-night pundits argue about whether a society should lean this hard on one man. The public knows him through his hero work and his interviews, and he never talks about his private life.

Names and Forms of Address.text: Names in Japan are spoken family name first and written that way on official forms, while this world's records list people given name first. Acquaintances, classmates, colleagues and strangers use family name plus a suffix: -san as the polite default, -kun for younger men and male classmates, -chan for small children, close friends and pets, -sama for customers and people of high status, sensei for teachers, doctors and some veteran pros, and senpai for an upperclassman at school or a senior at work. Moving to someone's given name is a real step in a friendship and usually happens by invitation; dropping the suffix shows closeness, or rudeness from a stranger. On the job pros go by their hero names: the public, the press and colleagues say Endeavor or Mount Lady, and a hero's legal name, though on record, is seldom used. Students address teachers by hero name or as sensei. A childhood nickname used by only one person marks a long shared history. Bows replace handshakes: a nod between friends, a deeper bow for thanks, apologies and superiors. Every canon person keeps exactly the forms of address their own record uses.

Hero Names and Costumes.text: A hero name is the name a pro works under, and Hero Course students choose theirs during their first year as part of their training. A name should say what kind of hero someone means to be; a teacher can send back one that is embarrassing, misleading or already taken, and it becomes official when the Hero Public Safety Commission registers it with a license. Until then students go by their own names. Hero costumes are designed by the hero and built by support companies: every Hero Course student files a costume request with measurements, Quirk details and sketches on enrollment, and U.A.'s partner companies deliver the finished costumes in numbered cases. A costume is protective gear first and an image second: fabric suited to the Quirk, armor where the body takes impact, built-in support items, and colors the public will remember. Changes go through the Development Studio or the original company, and Support Course students compete for the work. Licensed heroes own their costumes, register any support item that could serve as a weapon, and pay to replace what villains wreck. A costume licenses nobody: a costumed person using a Quirk in public without a license is a vigilante in the eyes of the law.

Healing and Medical Care.text: Quirk healing is rare, hard to train and never free, so ordinary medicine does most of the work of keeping heroes alive. At U.A. Academy, Recovery Girl heals injuries with a kiss that speeds the patient's own healing; it draws on the patient's stamina, so a badly hurt student wakes exhausted, and she refuses to keep patching anyone who returns from the same recklessness, leaving them to mend the slow way. She cannot regrow what is lost or cure illness. Elsewhere ambulances, hospitals and doctors work as they do anywhere in Japan, with Quirk specialists at the big hospitals for injuries caused by Quirks and for patients whose bodies follow unusual rules. Recovery takes real time: a broken bone means weeks in a cast or splint, a concussion means rest and no training, burns need their dressings changed. Pros carry first aid kits, and larger agencies keep a doctor on call. Every Quirk injury treated at a hospital is reported to the police, so villains avoid hospitals and pay unlicensed doctors found through brokers. Hospitals post guards on patients under arrest, and a hero hurt in the line of duty gets a stream of visitors, flowers and cameras at the entrance.

Money, Work and Pay.text: Yen pays for everything, and most people earn it the ordinary way: salaried office jobs, shifts in shops and restaurants, deliveries, factories and building sites. A part-time job pays roughly 1,000 to 1,300 yen an hour, settled on payday; a convenience-store snack costs a few hundred yen, a restaurant meal 500 to 1,500, a local train ride a few hundred, and a month's rent for a small city apartment tens of thousands. U.A. students live in Heights Alliance and pay for what they buy outside it (cafeteria meals, food, phones, clothes, weekends in town) from family money or a part-time job. Pro heroes are paid a public-service fee for each case they resolve, on top of their agency's income from merchandise, endorsements and appearances, which is why case credit is money; sidekicks draw salaries from the agency. Police officers and teachers are salaried public servants. Villains live on cash jobs paid through brokers, stolen goods sold to fences and debts owed to people who collect. Once a price, a wage or a debt is named it stays fixed, and nobody is paid for attending a lesson or for doing the right thing.

Disasters and Emergency Response.text: Japan lives with earthquakes, typhoons, floods, landslides and fires, and its emergency system is older than the hero system and still runs every disaster. Phones blare national alerts, sirens and loudspeakers order evacuations, schools and offices drill every year, and every neighborhood has a marked evacuation site, usually a school ground or a park. Fire departments, police and city crews run the response; rescue heroes are called in by agency or by name, and the first pro on scene reports to the incident commander. Rescue specialists are among the most respected pros: Thirteen, the Wild Wild Pussycats and every hero whose Quirk can dig, fly, lift, cool or sense. The order never changes: get people out, treat the injured, stop the spread, then clear and rebuild. Unlicensed people may carry, guide and give first aid, but a Quirk used in a rescue without a license still brings a police statement afterward. Typhoons come in late summer and autumn with a day or two of warning; earthquakes come with none. Afterward shelters fill, trains stop, convenience stores empty, volunteers arrive, and the news replays footage of the heroes who were there.

Quirk Overuse.text: Quirk overuse means pushing a Quirk past what the user's body can carry, and the body pays at once. The warning signs come first and depend on the Quirk: shaking hands, a pounding headache, a nosebleed, nausea, blurred sight, skin that burns or goes numb, a power that sputters or overshoots. Past those signs the damage turns real: torn muscle, cracked or broken bone, burns on the user's own skin, fainting, and in the worst cases internal injury or a Quirk that misfires for days afterward. Overuse injuries heal at the body's own pace. Healing Quirks shorten the time but do not erase the cost, and a body hurt the same way again and again can carry the damage for life. Doctors, teachers and agencies treat a user who keeps overusing a Quirk as a safety risk: in a hero academy, repeated overuse earns a stern talk, benched training or a medical hold long before it earns praise. A single overuse in a true emergency is understood; making a habit of it is called reckless.

Quirk Exhaustion.text: Quirk exhaustion is the drained state that follows long or heavy Quirk use, and only rest, food and sleep end it. Nothing is torn or broken, but the Quirk weakens, slows, loses range and sometimes fails to start, while the user turns hungry, cold, clumsy and sleepy. Quirks that burn a fuel run out first, and their users need exactly what they spent: sugar, water, fat or salt. Ordinary exhaustion clears after a meal and a night's rest; a full day at a Quirk's limit can take two or three days to shake off. Healing that draws on the patient's stamina helps an exhausted body least. Heroes plan shifts, carry supply packs and hand off before they run dry, because a pro working on an empty Quirk gets people hurt. Hero students learn the feeling early, and their dorm kitchens see enormous dinners after training.

Quirk Practice Facilities.text: Quirk practice facilities are licensed gyms and halls where anyone may use a Quirk legally under supervision, and most civilians train their powers there. Cities run public ones and companies run private ones: reinforced rooms with fireproof walls, drains and padded floors, outdoor ranges outside town for large or loud Quirks, pools for water users. Certified instructors check each visitor's registered Quirk at the desk, assign a suitable room and set the session's limits. Visitors book by the hour, sign a waiver and spar only with staff present. Counselors refer children with hard-to-control powers to classes there, and hero academy applicants fill the evening slots. A Quirk used outside the booked room, in the parking lot or on the walk home, counts as public use again.

Effects of Quirk Suppression.text: When a Quirk is suppressed, the power stops at its source, but whatever it already did stays done. An Emitter stops producing its effect at once: no new flame, current or force comes out. A fire it already lit keeps burning, a thrown object keeps flying and an object it already created stays real. Effects that need the user's continued power, such as a held barrier, a floating load, a moving shadow or a grip that keeps something in place, collapse the moment suppression lands, which makes suppressing a user in midair or under a heavy load dangerous. A Transformation ends and the body returns to its normal form. A Mutant body does not change at all: gills, wings, claws, strength and senses that are part of the body stay, because they are anatomy, not a power being switched on. A suppressed person feels the Quirk go silent and gets it back with no lasting harm when the suppression ends. Suppression never touches training, weapons, gear or plain muscle, so a suppressed fighter can still fight. Erasure-type Quirks, restraint devices and suppression gear all follow this rule, and heroes and officers plan for what remains after the power is gone.

Quirk Interactions.text: When two Quirks meet, the result follows the physical effects involved, not a rule that one power cancels another. Fire meeting ice makes steam and meltwater; electricity runs through water and metal and finds whoever stands in them; wind feeds a fire or blows it back; a hardened body takes a blast that would break an ordinary one; a barrier holds until the force against it exceeds what it can bear. Two strong effects colliding can release far more than either alone, and the overflow lands on whoever is nearby, which is why fights between Quirk users are so destructive. Combinations can be deliberate. Teammates who know each other's Quirks build combined moves, a wind user carrying a flame user's heat or a water user soaking a target for an electric user, and hero academies drill pairs for exactly that. Unfamiliar Quirks meeting by accident are unpredictable, so pros on a joint operation share their Quirks' basics before the work starts. When two Quirks together cause an accident, both users answer for their own part.

Heteromorph Health Care.text: Heteromorph health care is ordinary medicine adjusted to bodies that follow their own rules, and its quality depends on where a patient lives. Large hospitals keep Quirk specialists who can read an unusual heartbeat, set a bone in a wing, treat scales or fur and size a dose for a body far heavier, lighter or differently built than the textbook patient. Smaller clinics often lack the equipment: a blood-pressure cuff that does not fit, a scanner too narrow, a dentist with no plan for a beak or tusks. Many heteromorph families carry a file on their own body to every appointment. Public insurance covers specialist care, though rural patients may travel far for it. Sending a heteromorph patient to a veterinarian, or joking about it, is an insult that makes the news.

Accidental Quirk Activation.text: When a Quirk activates by accident, the law asks first whether anyone was careless. Accidents are common: a sneeze that throws sparks, a nightmare that frosts a bedroom, a flinch that sets off a power on a crowded train, a fever or a few drinks that loosen control. Children have the most accidents, but adults under stress, illness or exhaustion have them too. If nobody is hurt and nothing breaks, the moment usually ends with an apology. If there is harm or damage, someone calls the police, an officer takes a statement and checks the registry, and a genuine accident brings no criminal charge, though the user still pays for the damage, usually through insurance. Recklessness changes that: activating a known unstable Quirk in a crowd, skipping prescribed gear or ignoring a counselor's limits can bring a fine or a charge. Repeated accidents lead to mandatory Quirk counseling, a control device or restrictions at school or work. Accidents caught on camera spread online fast, and the user's face spreads with them.

The Chaos Years.text: The chaos years are the first decades after Quirks appeared, when no law, job or institution was built for people with powers and much of the world came apart. Quirk crime outran the police: robberies no lock could stop, gangs built around a few strong Quirks, towns where the strongest person nearby made the rules. Fear ran the other way too: mobs attacked people with frightening bodies, early heteromorphs were driven from homes and jobs, and courts could not say whether a Quirk was a weapon. Militant movements, the Meta Liberation Army the best remembered, fought the government over the right to use powers freely. Textbooks present the period as a warning, and its memory is why most people accept strict Quirk laws without complaint.

The First Heroes.text: The first heroes were ordinary people with Quirks who began protecting others on their own, before any license existed. During the chaos years some borrowed the idea from old comics: they took names, wore costumes, stopped robberies and pulled people from wrecks. They broke the law to do it, and many were hurt or arrested, but the public loved them, and in many towns they were the only help that came. Japan chose to license them rather than prosecute them: the best received legal standing, government pay and rules to follow, and the word hero passed from the street into the law. Those who refused the license or could not meet its standards became the first people the system called vigilantes. Hero history classes still open with these figures.

The Founding of Hero Law.text: Hero law was Japan's answer to the chaos years: ban dangerous Quirk use for everyone, then license a trained few to use their Quirks for the public. The criminal code alone had failed, because the police could not match the strongest offenders. The new laws made public Quirk use illegal without permission, required every Quirk to be registered, and created a profession of heroes paid by the state for the cases they resolve. The Hero Public Safety Commission was founded to run the system as a single authority, setting standards, approving hero courses and issuing licenses, while the police kept the power to arrest, investigate and detain. The framework has been amended many times, but its core has held for generations.

History of the Hero Rankings.text: The hero rankings began as a way for the public to judge heroes once there were too many to know by name. Magazines and television first ran popularity polls of their own, and arguments over the best hero filled talk shows.
