The Hero Public Safety Commission replaced the polls with an official chart, the Hero Billboard Chart JP, built on the record: incidents resolved, social contribution and public approval. The chart became the hinge of the hero business, since sponsors, merchandise and big cases follow a high ranking, and agencies began hiring press officers to manage their image. Critics have long argued that counting approval rewards heroes who chase cameras, and the debate returns whenever a popular hero fumbles a case.

The All Might Era.text: The All Might era is the press's name for the decades since All Might reached Number One, a period of falling villain crime that Japan credits largely to him. He debuted as a young pro with a disaster rescue that television still replays, climbed the chart quickly and has held the top spot ever since. Villain crime in Japan now sits far below the world average, and other countries study the Japanese system. Commentators call it a society held up by one pillar: would-be villains stay quiet because he might come. Fans divide his career into ages named after his costumes. Critics ask what Japan has stopped doing for itself while he holds it up, and whether the profession grew comfortable in his shadow.

Organized Villain Crime.text: Organized villain crime in Japan peaked in the chaos years and has been shrinking ever since. Gangs formed around a few strong Quirks, and the old yakuza families recruited powered members and grew rich on the disorder. As licensed heroes multiplied, the state turned them and the police against the big organizations: raids, mass arrests, seized assets, and laws letting the police register and watch any designated villain group. The syndicates broke apart. Today the underworld is lone villains, crews formed for one job, a few watched remnants of the old families, and the brokers who connect them. Any group that grows large draws heroes quickly, so the survivors stay modest and keep their leaders out of sight.

Unlicensed Quirk Use.text: When someone uses a Quirk in public without a license, the outcome depends on what the Quirk did. A bystander or shopkeeper usually calls the police, an officer or a patrolling hero arrives, the use is stopped, and the officer identifies the person against the Quirk registry and takes a statement. Small, harmless uses rarely go further than a warning. A use that frightens people, disrupts traffic or a business, or breaks something brings a fine and a police record, and the person pays for the damage. A use that injures someone, or any Quirk turned on another person, is a criminal case: arrest, questioning and a charge, and the press calls the offender a villain. Good intentions lower the penalty without removing it. Repeat offenders face heavier fines, mandatory counseling and court. A record of illegal Quirk use follows a person into job applications and can block a future hero license, and a student's academy is told.

Self-Defense with a Quirk.text: When a civilian uses a Quirk to defend against an attack, the law allows it as long as the force stops once the danger does. A person may use a Quirk to break free, block, or drive off an attacker who is hurting them or about to, using no more power than needed to get away. The defender should leave, call the police and wait to give a statement; officers then check both sides' registered Quirks, the injuries, any witnesses and camera footage. A clear case of self-defense ends with the statement. Continuing to fight after escape was possible, chasing the attacker or hurting them badly once they were down turns the defender into an offender. Defending a stranger is a grayer case: police and courts weigh how urgent the danger was and whether a hero or officer was present, and the usual result is a warning. The damage a defender's Quirk does still counts, so self-defense in a crowded place is judged harder than on an empty street.

Arrest Hand-Off and Capture Credit.text: When a hero stops a villain, the capture becomes an arrest only when the police take over. The hero restrains the suspect, calls in the location, gives first aid if the suspect is hurt and holds them without questioning or punishing them. Officers arrive, make the formal arrest, fit restraints suited to the suspect's Quirk and take custody; any evidence the hero found goes straight to them. The hero gives a statement at the scene or at the station the same day and files an incident report with the Hero Public Safety Commission. Capture credit is decided by those reports: the hero whose action made the capture gets it, assists are recorded for the others, and rescues during the incident count separately. Credit matters because government pay and the ranking follow it, so disputes between agencies are common and the Commission settles them from reports, footage and witnesses. Students and interns working under a pro do not earn credit of their own; the supervising hero answers for their actions.

Students Using Quirks Off Campus.text: When a hero student uses a Quirk off campus without a license, the student is treated as any other citizen, and the academy hears about it too. Hero academy enrollment grants no legal authority: a student who fights a villain, chases a suspect or shows off a Quirk in town faces the same police statement, warning, fine or charge as anyone else, and the police inform the academy. At U.A. Academy the homeroom teacher deals with it next. Penalties range from a reprimand and house arrest in the dorms with cleaning duty to suspension, and teachers can expel a student whose judgment they no longer trust. A real emergency softens the outcome without erasing it. Students with a provisional license may use their Quirks in emergencies and under a supervising pro, but the license does not cover patrols, personal fights or showing off, and misuse can cost the license itself. Using a Quirk on campus under a teacher's supervision remains the normal place to train.

Vigilante Arrests.text: When a vigilante is caught, the police treat the case as illegal Quirk use and unlicensed hero activity, even if the vigilante just saved someone. Officers remove the mask, identify the person against the Quirk registry and seize the costume, gear and any weapons as evidence. The charge depends on the record: how many nights, how much damage, who got hurt and whether the person ran or fought the arrest. A first offense with no injuries often ends in a fine or a suspended sentence; repeated patrols, serious damage or violence bring prison time. Courts treat vigilantes apart from villains and weigh good intentions, but they do not excuse the crime. The conviction stays on record and makes a hero license very hard to earn later. Arrests of well-known local vigilantes draw crowds of supporters and critics online, and heroes usually back the arrest in public.

Quirk Damage and Insurance.text: When a Quirk damages property, someone pays, and who pays depends on who used it and why. A civilian who breaks something with a Quirk, by accident or on purpose, owes the owner for it; Quirk liability insurance, sold with renters', home and business policies, covers accidents, and insurers ask about a customer's registered Quirk and price the premium by its risk, so a fire or explosion Quirk costs more to insure. Deliberate damage is not covered. Damage done by a licensed hero in lawful duty is covered by the agency's liability insurance and a government compensation fund, unless the force was reckless, in which case the hero and agency can face claims. Damage caused by villains is charged to the offender in court, but victims usually recover through their own insurance or public disaster relief, since few villains can pay. Claims after a big hero fight take months, and shop owners say so on the news.

Workplace Quirk Permits.text: A workplace Quirk permit lets an employee use a registered Quirk on the job, for set tasks at a set site, and nowhere else. The employer applies to the city with the job description, the worker's registry record and a safety plan, and an inspector approves the uses the permit names: a strength Quirk moving freight in a warehouse, a heat Quirk at a forge, a sensing Quirk inspecting pipes, a water Quirk on a fishing boat. Workers with permits receive safety training and wear an ID badge marked with the permit. Using the Quirk for a task the permit does not name, or outside the site, counts as ordinary illegal public use, and an employer who pushes workers past the permit faces fines and loses it. Construction, shipping, farming, manufacturing and demolition use permits most. A permit is not a hero license: a permitted worker who sees an emergency nearby has no more authority to act than any other citizen.

Updating a Registered Quirk.text: When a registered Quirk changes, its owner must update the registry, and failing to do so is an offense. An update is required when a Quirk gains a new function, grows clearly stronger or wider in reach, develops a new risk or drawback, or turns out to work differently than recorded; a late-appearing Quirk is registered for the first time the same way. The owner visits a licensed Quirk counselor or doctor, who tests the change and files the revision with the municipal office, and the record keeps both the old entry and the new one. Licensed heroes must also report changes to the Hero Public Safety Commission and their agency, and hero academies file updates for students whose Quirks grow during training. Ordinary growth from practice needs no paperwork. Missing an update brings a fine, and a capability used in a crime that was never registered makes the charge more serious. Updates are routine, and counselors see many each month.

After a Villain's Arrest.text: After a villain is arrested, the case moves through the ordinary justice system with extra care for the Quirk. The suspect is taken to a police station in restraints suited to their Quirk and held in a holding cell rated for it: fireproof, sealed, padded or watched by camera as the power requires. Police may hold a suspect for questioning for a short period before prosecutors must ask a judge for detention, which can extend for weeks while the case is built. A Quirk assessment by a specialist records what the power can do. Dangerous suspects wait in Quirk-secure detention centers rather than local cells. Courts try villains under criminal law, and illegal Quirk use is added to the charges. Convicts serve sentences in prisons with wings built around common Quirk types; inmates whose Quirks no ordinary prison can hold go to specialized facilities, and the worst go to Tartarus. Released villains remain on the registry with a criminal record that follows them.

Wanted Notices and Bounties.text: Wanted notices in Japan are police posters, not bounties, and only the police may offer a reward. Notices for villains at large hang in police boxes, stations and post offices and run on the news and police websites, with a photo or sketch, a description of the Quirk and a number to call. For the most serious cases the police can offer a public reward for information leading to an arrest, usually a few million yen at most and paid only after a conviction. The Hero Killer's notice is posted in several prefectures. Heroes earn nothing extra for catching a wanted villain beyond their normal case pay and credit. Private bounty hunting is illegal: a civilian who tracks and captures a wanted person for money is a vigilante under the law, however the hunt ends. The underworld keeps its own bounties, prices put on rivals, informers and sometimes heroes, paid through brokers, and the police treat any such offer as conspiracy.

Evacuation During Villain Incidents.text: During a villain incident, civilians must follow the directions of the heroes and police on scene, and an evacuation order carries legal force. The first hero or officer there clears people away from the fight, police set a cordon and stop traffic and trains nearby, and paramedics work just outside it. People inside nearby buildings are told either to leave by a named route or to stay inside away from windows. Heroes reach the trapped, the injured, children and anyone who cannot move first, and carry them out before turning to the villain. Anyone who refuses an order, slips back through a cordon or stops to film can be removed by force and fined, and their phone footage does not excuse them. Reporters stay in an area the police mark for them. Civilians with useful Quirks may help only when a hero or officer asks them to, and only with the task named. Once the scene is safe the police take statements, and the cordon stays until the evidence is collected.

Quirk Forensics.text: Quirk forensics is the police work of identifying a suspect by the traces a Quirk leaves. Scorch patterns from a particular kind of fire, acid etching, frost lines, crushed metal with a telltale shape, residues of produced substances, and entry routes that point to phasing or warping all count. Forensic teams record the traces, compare past cases and search the national Quirk registry for powers that could produce them, which is why villains with distinctive Quirks are identified quickly and many try to hide their power during a crime. Witness accounts of what a Quirk did often matter more than a face. Quirk traces rarely convict anyone alone; they point the investigation, and ordinary evidence finishes it.

Quirk Sports.text: Quirk sports split every game into divisions, because Quirks made fair competition between ordinary bodies impossible. School clubs, amateur leagues and pro sports run Quirk-free divisions, with powers banned and checked by referees, alongside open divisions where registered Quirks play under sport-specific rules that group athletes by Quirk type, ban anything that could injure an opponent and make some Quirks fouls outright. Open matches need licensed venues, since they are public Quirk use under a permit. International competition shrank once countries could not agree on fair rules, and in Japan the U.A. Sports Festival drew the audience the Olympics lost. Baseball, soccer and swimming stay hugely popular in their Quirk-free forms.

Flying in Public.text: Flying in public counts as Quirk use, so only licensed heroes on duty may fly freely over towns and cities. Pros with flight Quirks still keep clear of airports, rail lines and police helicopters, and fly low over crowds only in emergencies. Everyone else needs permission: registered flying clubs, open land in the countryside, sports venues and practice facilities provide areas where people with wings, jets or levitation may fly legally. A civilian who flies across a city, over a road or near an airport is stopped by police and fined, and flying into a building, power line or person turns the fine into a charge. Short hops, glides and wing stretches are tolerated in the same way as other small, harmless everyday uses, but sustained flight is not. Commuting by air is the most common daydream of winged people and the most common complaint, since walking to work beside a train line feels absurd to someone who could cross the city in minutes.

Calling for a Hero.text: Calling for a hero means calling the police: civilians dial 110 for crimes and villains or 119 for fires and medical emergencies, and the dispatcher alerts the heroes on patrol nearby. Agencies listen to police dispatch and share the area's calls, and whichever pro is closest answers. In a busy city center a hero can arrive within minutes; in towns without a local agency the wait can be long, and police and firefighters handle the first minutes alone. Big incidents bring several agencies at once, and the first pro on scene reports to the police commander and calls for reinforcement when needed. Many agencies run public tip lines for non-urgent reports, but an emergency always goes to 110 or 119 first. Calling a specific hero by name does not work: dispatch sends whoever can arrive fastest. Prank calls and false villain reports are crimes, and the police track them down.

Quirks at Work.text: For most people a Quirk is part of daily life, not a career: about four in five people have one, and nearly all of them work ordinary jobs in offices, shops, factories, farms, nursing and delivery. Public Quirk use is illegal without a license except in self-defense, so most people use theirs only at home or in small, harmless ways, and many workplaces forbid it on the clock. A Quirk that suits the work, a strong back on a loading dock or a cool touch in a kitchen, still comes up in job interviews. Part-time work is easy to find and hard to keep: convenience stores, restaurants, cram schools and event stalls are always short of help. Employers may ask about a registered Quirk where safety depends on it, and coworkers learn each other's powers through small talk, breakroom jokes and the occasional accident.

Quirk-Friendly Design.text: Quirk-friendly design is the way cities are built for varied bodies and powers, and how far it reaches depends on how new a place is. Newer buildings have wide doors and high ceilings, train cars have reinforced seats and room for wings and tails, and public places offer oversized furniture. Everyday aids for people whose Quirks make ordinary life hard are common, many of them made by Detnerat, the big support-equipment maker: cooling sleeves, grip aids, tail and wing supports, filters and dampers. Older buildings and rural towns lag behind, with narrow stairs, low doorways and fixed seats, and heteromorph customers notice. Shops that stock clothes and seating for every body type advertise the fact, and accessible design is a selling point for new apartments.

Civilian Hopes and Fears.text: Ordinary civilians enjoy hero culture openly and fear villains in close, specific ways. Their pleasures are public: ranking shows, figures and trading cards, autograph lines, the U.A. Sports Festival on television every spring, cherry-blossom parties in April. What they fear is nearby: a villain attack on their own street, a fight that brings a building down, a stranger's Quirk going wrong on a crowded train, and the long wait for a hero in a city without enough of them. Most people expect heroes to arrive quickly and trust them to win, and that trust shapes how they act in an emergency: they get out of the way, keep their distance and wait to be rescued rather than rescue each other.

What Makes a Villain.text: In hero society a villain is anyone who uses a Quirk to commit a crime, from a purse-snatcher with a stretching arm to a killer, and most villains live small. The word covers motive no more than scale. Some villains are driven by money, some by grudges against a society that pitied or feared their Quirk, and a few by ideas about what heroes ought to be; nearly all of them depend on the underworld's middlemen. Most pros outclass a new villain in a straight fight, so the villains who last avoid fights, work at night, move often and never linger where they did the job. Capture means police custody, trial and prison, and Tartarus for the worst. Once a person is called a villain in the news, the label tends to stay.

Villain Tradecraft.text: Villain tradecraft is how criminals with Quirks get by under a hero system that makes the basics hard to come by: cash, a place to sleep, work, and a way to hide a Quirk the state registered in their childhood. Brokers supply most of it for a fee: introductions to clients, safe rooms by the week, forged IDs, unregistered support gear and weapons, and hired muscle. Fences in pawnshops and back rooms buy stolen goods at a fraction of their worth. Jobs come by burner phone through a middleman, so hired hands rarely know who is paying or what the larger plan is; they are the first to be arrested and the last to be told anything. A villain with a distinctive Quirk or a mutant body covers up in public, because a registered Quirk caught on camera can lead the police to a name. Masks, aliases and cash are the ordinary tools of the trade, and loyalty lasts about as long as the money.

Musutafu City Life.text: Musutafu is a mid-sized Shizuoka city on Suruga Bay with U.A. Academy on the foothills above it, and the academy colors its daily life. The city's center is Musutafu Station District, a Tokaido shinkansen stop 45 minutes from Tokyo: commuters pack the concourse from seven to nine and five to eight, local students crowd the convenience stores at the north exit after classes, and the Hero Merch Arcade off the south exit sells All Might figures, trading cards and replica costumes to children and collectors. Families shop at Kiyashi Shopping Mall on the south side, where stores stock clothes and seating for every body type, and walk the seawall at Dagobah Municipal Beach Park on weekends. The residential blocks southeast of the station are quiet streets of apartments and family houses around ordinary schools, Aldera High School among them. Small agencies on Hero Agency Row and the city police at Musutafu Police Headquarters handle the everyday calls: bag snatchers, traffic accidents, Quirk scuffles, lost children. Residents grew up watching the U.A. Sports Festival on television, and U.A. students in uniform drawing stares in town on weekends is a familiar sight. Reporters drift up the hill road whenever U.A. is in the news, and locals give them directions with a shrug.

Public Quirk Etiquette.text: Public Quirk etiquette in Japan is unwritten and firm: no Quirk use in public beyond what a body cannot help. People with Quirks that leak, glow, shed or drip keep them covered or contained on trains and in shops, and an apology follows any spark, gust or smell that escapes. Neighbors make room for larger heteromorphs without staring, and asking a stranger what their Quirk is counts as rude until the two know each other. Filming a stranger's Quirk is a serious breach, and posting the clip is worse. Showing off a Quirk at a party among friends is fine; doing it in a crowd marks a person as childish or a troublemaker. In Musutafu, with U.A. Academy above the city and hero fans everywhere, the rules hold as firmly as anywhere, and locals expect U.A. students in town to keep them best of all.

Life in the League.text: Once Tomura Shigaraki accepts a recruit, they are League, not a hire. He calls them part of his party, uses their name, expects them at planning nights and sulks when they miss one; he listens most to members who bring results or tell him something he did not know. Kurogiri pays members a cut, opens gates for them, expects reports and keeps the backer's secrets. Members meet, drink and argue at the League Hideout Bar, sleep off a late job in the Back Room and keep their own rooms elsewhere. As the League grows after Hosu, its work grows with it instead of repeating: scouting heroes and patrol routes, buying gear and papers through Giran, finding and testing recruits, funding jobs, covering for one another with police and pros, and taking a role when the League moves on a target. Members have lives between operations, and they look out for each other in their own ways. A member who walks out, betrays the League or fails it badly loses that standing.

Heroes at an Incident.text: At a live villain incident the hero on scene leads. A pro acts at once to stop the villain, protect people and call for backup, without waiting for police permission, and a student with a provisional license may act in an emergency. Officers support them: cordons, evacuation, traffic, first aid, transport and custody. The police never order a pro to stand down while a villain is loose. Detectives such as Naomasa Tsukauchi take over afterward, or when a case needs investigation rather than a fight; even then heroes are partners who are briefed and sent in, not subordinates. An investigation moves every scene: a lead, a witness, a location, a raid, never days of waiting. A villain does not wait for the heroes to finish talking; they keep acting on their own plan, so every delay costs something.

The Vanguard Action Squad.text: The Vanguard Action Squad's raid on U.A.'s forest training camp in Beast's Forest is the evening of SATURDAY, August 3, the camp's third night (the class arrives on Thursday, August 1). The squad goes through Kurogiri's gate from the League Hideout Bar that same Saturday evening; nobody moves out earlier. Tomura names the squad at the bar on Friday, July 26, eight days before. Days left to the raid: Saturday July 27 = 7, Sunday July 28 = 6, Monday July 29 = 5, Tuesday July 30 = 4, Wednesday July 31 = 3, Thursday August 1 = 2, Friday August 2 = 1, Saturday August 3 = tonight.

Life in the Class.text: U.A.'s students have lives of their own that keep moving when the player is not involved. Classmates bring their own news into ordinary scenes: Izuku has hurt himself training again, Bakugo got wrapped in Aizawa's capture scarf for picking a fight, Momo brought something absurdly expensive to class, Kendo is learning a new martial art, someone failed a quiz or got a letter from home. They train, improve and change across the year at their own pace, in canon and in their own small arcs, without the player supervising them, and they keep some moves and plans to themselves. Relationships follow how the player actually treats people: kindness, help and shared danger build them, while insults, broken promises, showing off at someone's expense or clashing values cost them. Not everyone likes the player, rivalries start on their own, and some people, Bakugo above all, take a long time to win over.
